::: {.lead}

openEO machine-learning processes keep feature preparation and inference close to the data. Their availability is more backend-specific than core cube processes.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Backend support overview

The buttons on this page are a documentation aid, not a live capability registry. Use the [openEO Hub](https://hub.openeo.org/) for a cross-backend overview: open **Filters**, select a process under **Processes**, and the Hub shows only matching services. The Hub data is crawled and cached.
:::

::: {.tag-filter-item data-tags="vito"}
## A typical ML workflow

1. Create a feature cube with processes such as `ndvi`, `aggregate_temporal_period`, and `filter_bands`.
2. Train a supported model or load an exported model, depending on the backend.
3. Apply it with a model-prediction process and export the resulting cube.

### Python

```python
# Feature preparation stays portable across backends.
features = (
    cube.filter_bands(["B02", "B03", "B04", "B08"])
    .aggregate_temporal_period(period="month", reducer="median")
)

# The available training and prediction methods must be checked per backend.
processes = connection.list_processes()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Check before building the workflow

Look for processes such as `fit_class_random_forest`, `fit_regr_random_forest`, `predict_random_forest`, `load_ml_model`, or `predict_ml_model` in the connected backend's process listing. Exact names and supported model formats may differ by process specification version.
:::
:::

## Machine-learning process details

Each model process is documented separately because training, loading, and prediction support can differ between backends.

::: {.tag-filter-item data-process="fit_class_random_forest"}
## Train a random-forest classifier

Use `fit_class_random_forest` when labelled training features should be used to classify a feature cube. The backend determines the supported feature layout, label column, and model parameters.

```python
model = training_data.fit_class_random_forest(target_column="class")
```
:::

::: {.tag-filter-item data-process="fit_regr_random_forest"}
## Train a random-forest regressor

Use `fit_regr_random_forest` when labelled training features contain a continuous target such as biomass or temperature. Check the backend metadata for required training dimensions and parameter names.

```python
model = training_data.fit_regr_random_forest(target_column="value")
```
:::

::: {.tag-filter-item data-process="predict_random_forest"}
## Predict with a random forest

Use `predict_random_forest` after preparing a feature cube with the same bands and ordering used for training. It returns model predictions aligned with the input features.

```python
prediction = features.predict_random_forest(model=model)
```
:::

::: {.tag-filter-item data-process="load_ml_model"}
## Load a machine-learning model

Use `load_ml_model` when a model has already been stored in the backend and should be reused by a new workflow. Model identifiers, permissions, and formats are backend-specific.

```python
model = connection.load_ml_model(model_id="my-model")
```
:::

::: {.tag-filter-item data-process="save_ml_model"}
## Save a machine-learning model

Use `save_ml_model` to persist a trained model for later prediction or sharing within the backend workspace. Confirm retention and access rules before using it in production.

```python
saved = model.save_ml_model(model_id="my-model")
```
:::

::: {.tag-filter-item data-process="predict_ml_model"}
## Predict with a generic model

Use `predict_ml_model` when the backend supports a generic model format that is not covered by a specialized process. Exact model formats, input schema, and output labels must be checked in backend metadata.

```python
prediction = features.predict_ml_model(model=model)
```
:::

::: {.tag-filter-item data-process="predict_onnx"}
## Predict with an ONNX model

Use `predict_onnx` to apply a portable ONNX model when the backend advertises ONNX inference. The model input order and tensor shape must match the feature cube.

```python
prediction = features.predict_onnx(model=model)
```
:::
